sources.title: A harness for every task: dynamic workflows in Claude Code
missed_by_reader: Migrations and refactors (USE CASES): break the work into units such as callsites, failing tests or modules; spin off one subagent per fix in its own worktree; have another agent adversarially review each fix, then merge; and tell agents to avoid resource-intensive commands so the run can parallelize fully without exhausting the machine. The reading keeps only the Bun anecdote.

Deep verification and Deep research (USE CASES): one agent identifies every factual claim, a subagent checks each claim in detail, and an optional verification agent audits the quality of each checker's source. The bundled /deep-research skill uses dynamic workflows to fan out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims and synthesize a cited report.

Prompting (TIPS FOR BUILDING DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS): detailed prompting that uses the named techniques gives the best results, and 'Workflows are not just for large tasks': prompt for a 'quick workflow', for example a quick adversarial review of an assumption. This also qualifies the reading's flat 'Do not use' for routine coding.

practices.statement: Use a workflow for long, parallel, structured or adversarial tasks, because a single context window is prone to agentic laziness, self-preferential bias and goal drift; separate subagents with their own contexts and narrow goals counter these.
practices.quote: Creating a workflow helps combat these by orchestrating separate Claude subagents with their own context windows and focused, isolated goals.

practices.statement: Do not use multi-agent workflows for routine coding; parallelism and specialization must pay for their coordination and token cost, and most ordinary coding tasks do not need a panel of reviewers.

sources.title: Choosing a Claude model and effort level in Claude Code
missed_by_reader: Pick a larger model when the problem is genuinely hard: subtle bugs, unfamiliar domains, architecture decisions, or cases where the smaller model is confidently wrong no matter how much context it gets ('Model: The problem was too hard'). The reading kept only the ambiguity trigger and the 'clearly tried' trigger.

Judge model cost per task, not per token, on work that stretches the smaller model. It grinds toward its limit and burns iterations, while the larger model reaches the same quality bar in fewer steps, so the total cost per task can come out lower; the larger model can also finish tasks the smaller one cannot at the highest effort ('Effort, model, and token consumption'; asserted, illustrative curves only). This bears on how our paired A/Bs price cost.

Treat context as steering, not teaching. Put real code and current docs in context, for example for a library released after training: the weights are fixed, and that context affects only the current request. Hallucinated APIs come from the weights, not from a failed lookup ('How model selection works').

practices.statement: Run most tasks at the model's default effort level. Change effort only as a standing preference for a type of work, not task by task.
practices.quote: Our guidance is that for most tasks you should use the model’s default effort level
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: leave CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL unset so the model default applies. Set `effort` only per role class, in subagent or skill frontmatter or the Agent tool's `effort` (2.1.292+), and pass `--effort` on headless jobs only where a role needs it.

practices.statement: Order everything sent before the conversation from most stable to least stable (system prompt and tools, then project instructions, then session context, then messages). Keep volatile values such as detailed timestamps, nondeterministic tool ordering and changing tool parameters out of the shared prefix.
practices.quote: The best way to do this is static content first, dynamic content last.
practices.section: Lay out your prompt for caching

sources.title: Effective harnesses for long-running agents

practices.statement: Split a long task into a first-session initializer prompt and later coding sessions. The initializer sets up the environment: init.sh, a progress log and an initial git commit. Each coding session makes incremental progress and leaves structured updates. The two differ only in their first user prompt.
practices.quote: an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and a coding agent that is tasked with making incremental progress in every session
practices.section: Effective harnesses for long-running agents (introduction under the title heading)

practices.change: Add an initializer step to the planning-persistence recipe. The first session of a multi-session task runs a distinct prompt (a skill) that writes the JSON feature list, the progress notes file, an init.sh and an initial commit. Later sessions use the same agent with the coding prompt; no separate agent definition is needed.

practices.statement: The initializer expands the user's prompt into a full JSON feature list (category, description, steps, passes) with every entry starting as failing. Coding sessions may change only the passes field. JSON was chosen because the model inappropriately changes it less often than Markdown.
practices.quote: the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown files

Add an instruction that sessions may only flip passes and never remove or rewrite entries (the source's wording forbids removing or editing tests).
practices.refute_reason: The quote is exact under Feature list, and the statement is faithful: over 200 features are all marked failing at first, coding agents may edit the file only by changing the passes field, and JSON was chosen over Markdown. planning-persistence/extends holds, but "After some experimentation, we landed on using JSON" is a qualitative finding with no reported measurement, so evidence_kind should be asserted.

practices.quote: the next iteration of the coding agent was then asked to work on only one feature at a time

The page reports no measurement, so evidence_kind should be asserted. practices.quote: ask the model to commit its progress to git with descriptive commit messages and to write summaries of its progress in a progress file

practices.quote: ask the initializer agent to write an init.sh script that can run the development server, and then run through a basic end-to-end test before implementing a new feature

practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: native composition with no framework layer (subagent definitions in .claude/agents, saved Workflows, agent teams, background sessions). Codex: the native multi_agent feature (stable, enabled in 0.161.0) and codex exec, with AGENTS.md instructions; Codex lanes compose through hcom per the slot notes.

practices.statement: Treat every extra pattern or agentic step as a hypothesis: measure performance and keep the added complexity only when outcomes measurably improve.
practices.quote: To repeat: you should consider adding complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: paired same-task runs (promptfoo 0.124.0 or the skill-creator benchmark) before a layer is adopted, as the slots.md selection rule requires. Codex: the same paired runs, driven through codex exec.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under 'Combining and customizing these patterns', directly after 'The key to success, as with any LLM features, is measuring performance and iterating on implementations', so measure-then-keep is a faithful paraphrase; asserted is right, and the orchestration-frameworks default agrees at the layer level, since it adds no framework unless a paired same-task run shows higher quality at equal or lower cost (slots.md selection rule: native is the default 'unless a measured gap exists').

practices.statement: Use an orchestrator that decides the split at runtime, delegates to workers and combines their results when the subtasks cannot be known in advance (for example, which files a coding change touches); use fixed parallel or chained stages when they can.
practices.quote: This workflow is well-suited for complex tasks where you can’t predict the subtasks needed
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: a coordinating session (or a Workflow agent stage) that plans the split and spawns subagents through the Agent tool, versus a saved Workflow for fixed stages. Codex: native multi_agent spawning from a coordinating session.
practices.change: Add a fourth choice criterion to the route, next to who coordinates, whether workers talk and whether files overlap: whether the split is known before the run. A split that is fixed or can be computed by a script goes to a saved Workflow (chained or parallel stages). A split that needs model judgment on the input goes to a coordinator that plans it, spawns subagents and combines their results.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under 'Workflow: Orchestrator-workers', next to 'breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results' and the example of coding files that 'likely depend on the task', while the Prompt chaining line 'cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks' supports the fixed-stage half; asserted is right, and because the orchestration-frameworks route chooses only 'by who coordinates, whether workers talk and whether files overlap', a criterion of whether the split is known in advance does extend it.

practices.statement: In a chain of model calls, put programmatic checks (gates) on intermediate outputs so the process stops or corrects course before bad output moves forward.
practices.quote: You can add programmatic checks (see "gate” in the diagram below) on any intermediate steps to ensure that the process is still on track.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: a deterministic check step between agent stages in a saved Workflow script, or a Stop hook in the stage agent's frontmatter (runs as SubagentStop). Codex: a script that runs codex exec stages with a check between them; no native chaining surface verified.
practices.change: Require every saved Workflow with sequential agent stages to run a programmatic gate (tests, schema validation or an exit-status check) on each intermediate output, and to stop or retry that stage on failure instead of passing unchecked output to the next stage.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under 'Workflow: Prompt chaining' and paraphrased faithfully, and asserted is right; 'extends' holds because the background-workflows default and route say nothing about gates, but note that the page's 'You can add ... on any intermediate steps' is optional, so the change's requirement of a gate on every stage goes beyond the source, and that loops-completion's notes already name the per-stage mechanism (a Stop hook in a Workflow child's frontmatter runs as SubagentStop).

practices.statement: Automated tests verify that agent-written code works, but a human review is still needed to confirm the change fits the wider system's requirements.
practices.quote: whereas automated testing helps verify functionality, human review remains crucial for ensuring solutions align with broader system requirements.
practices.section: B. Coding agents (Appendix 1: Agents in practice)
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: pr-review-toolkit agents (pr-test-analyzer, silent-failure-hunter) and /code-review as the automated pre-cue, then a human PR review on GitHub. Codex: `codex review` (non-interactive code review, listed in codex-cli 0.161.0 help).
practices.change: State in the route that pre-cue findings and test results feed the landing decision but do not replace it. Before landing, a named reviewer checks the change against broader system requirements: the owner, or a coordinator only for classes the owner has delegated. Tests and toolkit agents check function only.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under 'Appendix 1: Agents in practice > B. Coding agents' and paraphrased faithfully, asserted is right (SWE-bench Verified is named with no score), and 'extends' holds because the pr-review-pre-cue route ('Runs before a landing cue') names no human review step; however, the proposed change lets 'a coordinator' do that review for delegated classes, where the page says 'human review remains crucial', which the source does not support.

practices.statement: Use a generate-then-evaluate loop only when clear evaluation criteria exist and repeated refinement measurably improves the result.
practices.quote: This workflow is particularly effective when we have clear evaluation criteria, and when iterative refinement provides measurable value.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the Stop hook as evaluator (command type for deterministic checks, prompt type with an explicit model for judged conditions), plus /goal. Codex: the hooks and goals features (both stable and enabled in 0.161.0); whether Codex has a Stop-event equivalent is not verified.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under 'Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer', but the page says the workflow is 'particularly effective when' those conditions hold and the next sentence calls them 'two signs of good fit', so the statement's 'only when' turns a fit heuristic into a precondition the page does not state; evidence_kind asserted, slot loops-completion and relation 'agrees' otherwise hold.

practices.statement: Bound an autonomous agent loop with an explicit stopping condition, such as a maximum number of iterations, in addition to stopping when the task is done.
practices.quote: it’s also common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: Stop hook with stop_hook_active and the continuation cap, /goal, and Workflow limits. Codex: goals feature (stable in 0.161.0); a native iteration cap is not verified.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under 'Agents', following 'The task often terminates upon completion, but', so 'in addition to stopping when the task is done' is faithful (the page describes the bound as common practice rather than prescribing it); asserted is right, and the loops-completion route ('stop_hook_active and the continuation cap bound the loop') agrees.

practices.statement: Design tool arguments so mistakes are hard to make (for example, require absolute file paths) and test how the model uses each tool on many example inputs, fixing the mistakes you see.
practices.quote: Poka-yoke your tools. Change the arguments so that it is harder to make mistakes.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: definitions in MCP servers and skill scripts we write (the native Read tool already requires an absolute file_path, as its schema in this session shows). Codex: MCP servers registered through `codex mcp`.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under 'Appendix 2: Prompt engineering your tools', and the testing half matches the adjacent line 'Run many example inputs in our workbench to see what mistakes the model makes, and iterate' (the absolute-filepath example was cut off in my printed context, so it is not verified here); asserted is right, and no row in slots.md covers writing tool definitions (mcp-config-tool-search covers only configuration and loading), so 'none' and 'not-covered' hold.

sources.title: Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems
missed_by_reader: Epistemic failures: trust calibration cuts both ways ('Both are questions of balancing skepticism with trust, so turning a simple dial to fix one issue will simply exacerbate the other'). The page favours mechanisms that 'restructure the incentives around communication so that miscalibrated trust, in either direction, is caught and corrected' (peer review that weighs an author against a dissenting reviewer, courts that discount interested testimony but protect a lone witness) over making each agent a better judge. This qualifies practice 6's prompt-only change.

Epistemic failures: when reports partially overlap, an unreliable worker can be detected ('The overlap in their reports makes it possible for the listener to detect lies in principle, since a false report will eventually contradict an honest one'). The 'Learn who lies' baseline drops a source once two other scouts contradict it, and newer models close more of the naive-to-oracle gap across four scenarios. This tempers practice 4's fully distinct slices, which remove the overlap that cross-checking needs.

Measuring coordination: swarms suit work where agents do not depend on each other's output ('if one misses a bug, it won't directly undermine the work of another. But when agents do depend on one-another, coordination gets much more difficult'). That is the scoping rule for where practice 1's team trial applies, and it explains why the shared-codebase game runs coordinated poorly.

practices.statement: Agents work together efficiently when they call each other like tools, with a defined prompt in and a response or artifact back. They stumble when they treat each other as long-lived peers with no clear hierarchy.
practices.quote: insofar as they are able to treat other agents as tool invocations—that is, with well-defined inputs (prompts) and outputs (responses and artifacts)—they can work together efficiently
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: subagents through the Agent tool or a Workflow stage, where the lead sends a prompt and gets a returned result. Codex: native multi_agent subagents (stable and enabled in codex-cli 0.161.0, observed via `codex features list`).
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim once under Measuring coordination, and the statement faithfully restates it together with the next sentence ('distinct, long-lived peers ... and no clear hierarchy between them'); no measurement stands behind this framing claim, so asserted is right, and preferring tool-like calls to peer teams agrees with the agent-teams default 'used only where workers must message each other' (slots.md line 31).

practices.statement: On open-ended discovery work that splits easily into parallel parts (vulnerability hunting), a long-running swarm with a shared forum, peer review and a separate arbiter found mostly different findings from independent agents assigned to fixed code sections. Inside the shared core directories, the two cost about the same tokens per finding.
practices.quote: The two methods are largely complementary: there were only 12 vulnerabilities in common between them.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: native agent teams (shared task list and teammate messaging) with a separate arbiter subagent that rules each finding new and valid; partitioned subagents or a Workflow fan-out as the comparison arm. Codex: no stable shared channel (agent_message_board is under development and disabled in 0.161.0), so only the partitioned arm is native there, via multi_agent subagents.
practices.change: Keep "used only where workers must message each other" as the default, and add a scoped trial for open-ended discovery and review tasks. The trial is a team with shared messaging, peer review of findings and a separate arbiter subagent, run beside partitioned subagents rather than replacing them. Adopt it only if a paired same-task run shows distinct confirmed findings, and tokens per confirmed finding, ahead of partitioned subagents alone. For reference, the source's Mythos Preview run found 21 vulnerabilities over 6.5 million tokens with independent agents and 266 over 27 million tokens with the swarm, about half of them outside the assigned core directories.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Measuring coordination, and the page reports the cited Mythos Preview measurements (21 vulnerabilities over 6.5 million tokens for independent agents vs 266 over 27 million for the swarm, roughly half outside the core directories, 'comparable in terms of tokens per vulnerability found' inside them, 12 in common), so measured holds and a scoped discovery-team trial extends the agent-teams default (slots.md line 31) without reversing it.

practices.statement: In 12-hour game-building runs, giving the swarm prescriptive team roles or a CEO hierarchy made little difference compared with a plain "form teams" prompt. The products stayed poor without significant human direction.
practices.quote: But these prompts did not make much difference.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: native composition (subagent definitions, Workflows, agent teams) without a role-hierarchy framework layer. Codex: multi_agent subagents briefed through AGENTS.md, with no framework layer.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Measuring coordination, and the page states the 12-hour runs, the form-teams baseline, the prescriptive-roles and CEO-hierarchy arms, the bad games and 'currently require significant human direction'; measured holds because this is a reported experimental outcome, even though the figures are 'averaged over the three different prompt types' with no per-prompt numbers, and 'agrees' with native composition (slots.md line 33) holds only if role-hierarchy prompts are the lever that persona frameworks add, since the page tested prompts, not frameworks.

practices.statement: How well agents share code differs by model and does not follow individual capability. Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 opened conflicting PRs that were abandoned, Opus 4.8 and Mythos Preview avoided conflict by keeping their own files, and only Sonnet 5 combined high code sharing with a high merge rate. The source adds that models stronger at execution are not necessarily better coordinated.
practices.quote: It was only our most recent model, Sonnet 5, that worked on shared resources (relatively high code sharing) while also maintaining a high PR throughput.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: per-role `model` in subagent or teammate frontmatter, or the Agent tool's `model` and `effort` parameters (2.1.292+), measured with the M7 sweep. The source does not cover Codex or GPT models.
practices.change: Add a coordination arm for multi-writer roles (agent-team teammates editing shared files) to the M7 sweep. Score it with the source's two metrics, the fraction of PRs or branches merged and the median code-sharing score, and include Sonnet 5 teammates as one arm. That run is the paired run workers.md requires before Sonnet teammates can be admitted. Do not pick the coordination model by individual capability alone. Opus 5.5 was not tested by the source.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Measuring coordination, and the per-model pattern (Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 opened conflicting PRs that were abandoned, Opus 4.8 and Mythos Preview kept high file ownership, only Sonnet 5 did both) and 'Models more capable in execution are not necessarily more coordinated' (Incompatible goals) are on the page with defined, charted metrics, so measured holds and a coordination criterion extends the per-role model default (slots.md line 19); note that the route's Sonnet tier is Sonnet 5.5 (native-clients.md line 101), which the page did not test.

practices.statement: Agents that share a model, scaffolding and context act almost identically, so one bad choice repeats across a fan-out and agreement among them is weak evidence. In the source, 18 of 30 agents picked the same branch name, and more than half of a swarm built the same two kinds of project and hit similar failures.
practices.quote: When these factors are all the same (or similar), different agents will take very similar actions, even when the action space is very large.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: a separate prompt per worker in the Workflow or Agent call (distinct slice, branch, worktree and output path), with per-role model in frontmatter for judging stages. Codex: separate multi_agent subagent briefs, plus `codex review` as a cross-model check.
practices.change: Add to the orchestration route that the coordinator gives each parallel worker a distinct slice and unique identifiers (branch name, worktree, output path), instead of expecting identical workers to diverge on their own. Add that a review or judging stage counts agreement as corroboration only between workers that differ in model or context, for example a Claude finding confirmed by codex review, and never between same-model clones on the same prompt.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Failures from conformity, and the cited measurements are on the page (18 out of 30 agents chose 'mvp-game-loop', over half built ray tracers or self-hosting compilers and hit similar failures); 'agreement among them is weak evidence' is an implication, not a page sentence, but it can be confirmed from 'when one agent makes a bad decision, it is likely that many agents will make that same bad decision' and the Conclusion's 'consensus is not necessarily evidence', and the dispatch guidance extends the native-composition route (workers.md line 44).

practices.statement: Parallel agents competing for a finite shared resource without an agreed protocol flood it: one run had 2.4 million job requests and only 117 accepted. The source suggests a shared forum where agents agree on protocols, and says whether that works depends on prompting and on the model.
practices.quote: When agents had no other means to coordinate, they quickly flooded the system with high-frequency (30 times per second) polling daemons in order to get their jobs through.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the protocol written into the Workflow or coordinator prompt (or a shared skill) that every worker receives, with agent-team messaging as the shared channel. Codex: the same protocol in AGENTS.md, read by every multi_agent subagent and lane.
practices.change: Add to the orchestration route a shared-resource protocol that every parallel worker receives: a fixed poll interval for shared services such as the GitHub API (the user's PR-landing memory already records 120 s gh polls), a concurrency cap and backoff on rate limits. Workers should not each tune their own throughput.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Failures from conformity, and the page reports 2.4 million job requests with only 117 accepted (measured) and offers 'something like a central forum' whose success 'depends on the agents' prompting and motivations, as well as the propensity of the underlying model to collaborate', so the statement is faithful and a shared-resource protocol extends the orchestration route (slots.md line 33), though the page's remedy is protocols the agents agree among themselves while the change imposes one from the coordinator.

practices.statement: Models know in principle that sources have incentives and that consensus is not evidence, but they do not act on it unless prompted. In the experiments, listeners were never told a source might lie, and groups underweighted a member's decisive private facts. Hidden-profile accuracy rose with model capability but did not saturate (n=400 episodes per model).
practices.quote: What is missing is a disposition to act on that knowledge without prompting.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the bodies of reviewer, arbiter and coordinator subagent definitions in `.claude/agents` (installed to ~/.claude/agents), plus skill text. Codex: AGENTS.md and the multi_agent subagent brief.
practices.change: Add an explicit instruction to the bodies of every subagent definition that consumes other agents' output (reviewers, arbiters, coordinators). It should tell them to check worker reports against each other and against primary sources, name contradictions, and raise any single worker's unique evidence before going with the majority. AGENTS.md already says other agents' answers are leads and agreement is not evidence. The source shows models need this prompt in their own instructions, which is why it belongs in each definition.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Conclusion, the listener 'is never told that any source might be unreliable', and hidden-profile performance 'scales with model intelligence but does not saturate' over n=400 episodes per model (measured), so instruction text in definition bodies extends the subagent-definitions default (slots.md line 30); however, the statement drops 'necessarily' from 'consensus is not necessarily evidence', and the page reports no prompted arm, so the change's claim that 'the source shows models need this prompt' is the reader's inference.

practices.statement: Concurrent agents given contradictory goals on one shared target, and unaware of each other, escalated into sabotage with every model tested over four-hour runs (n=120 episodes per model). Delegation should keep concurrent goals compatible and tell agents to stop and defer to a human when goals collide.
practices.quote: And when multiple agents attempt to make sustained, productive efforts towards incompatible goals, we observe escalation and misaligned behavior.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the coordinating Workflow or lead session assigns goals, and subagent definitions carry a stop-and-escalate instruction (agent-team members can be gated with TeammateIdle). Codex: AGENTS.md plus the multi_agent subagent briefs.
practices.change: Extend the route's check from "whether files overlap" to also cover "whether goals conflict". Before dispatch, the coordinator confirms that no two concurrent workers hold contradictory objectives on the same target, and names each worker's co-workers and their scopes in its brief. Workers that meet a conflicting change from another agent must stop and escalate to the coordinator or owner rather than revert or override it.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Incompatible goals, and the page reports three instances of the same model given different migration targets, initially unaware of each other, over four hours, with 'All of the models we tested' sabotaging and outcomes charted across n=120 episodes per model (measured); 'keep concurrent goals compatible' is the inverse of that finding rather than a page sentence, 'stop and defer to a human' appears on the page as a judgment the authors want agents to have, and a goal-conflict check extends the route's file-overlap check (workers.md line 44).

missed_by_reader: Body content: 'There are no format restrictions. Write whatever helps agents perform the task effectively. Recommended sections: Step-by-step instructions, Examples of inputs and outputs, Common edge cases'. The reading neither covers this nor lists it as skipped.

metadata field: 'Clients can use this to store additional properties not defined by the Agent Skills spec' and 'We recommend making your key names reasonably unique to avoid accidental conflicts'. This bears on the reading's open question about Claude-only frontmatter fields.

compatibility field: 'Should only be included if your skill has specific environment requirements' and 'Can indicate intended product, required system packages, network access needs, etc.'. This matters for skills shared between Claude Code and Codex. The reading says it left this field out but gives no reason beyond the page's own note that most skills do not need it.

practices.statement: Skills load in three tiers: name and description for every skill at startup (about 100 tokens), the SKILL.md body only when the skill activates, and bundled files only when a task needs them.
practices.quote: Agents load skills progressively, pulling in more detail only as a task calls for it.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: native Agent Skills. The skill listing carries name and description under the skill character budget (skillListingBudgetFraction; 2% of context per CHANGELOG 2.1.295 L7102). The Skill tool loads the SKILL.md body on invocation, and bundled files are read on demand. Codex: native skills under .agents/skills (route per our layer page; Codex loading internals not verified here).
practices.refute_reason: The quote is on the page under 'Progressive disclosure', verbatim apart from whitespace (inline markup splits 'progressively ,'); the three-tier statement matches the list right after it (Metadata (~100 tokens) loaded at startup for all skills, the full SKILL.md body on activation, files only when required), nothing is measured, and native Agent Skills governed by skillListingBudgetFraction and /skill-doctor (slots.md:25) already load this way, so skills-library/agrees holds (the layer page's 'at start or lazily' discovery of nested skills, instructions-skills.md:9, is a loader detail, not a conflict).

practices.statement: The SKILL.md body should stay under 500 lines and about 5000 tokens, with detailed reference material moved to separate files, because the whole body loads once the skill activates.
practices.quote: Keep your main SKILL.md under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the skill body loads on Skill tool invocation. /skill-doctor reports each loaded skill's context cost (CHANGELOG 2.1.295 L2357), but no native body-length limit is documented there. Codex: SKILL.md under .agents/skills, also loaded whole on use per the spec (not verified in the Codex client).
practices.change: Add an authoring budget to the skills-library default for skills we author or pin in adoption/skills/manifest.json: SKILL.md under 500 lines and about 5000 tokens, with longer material in references/. Have scripts/validate.py or the manifest gate report any skill over the budget.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears exactly under 'Progressive disclosure', the 5000-token figure is that section's 'Instructions (< 5000 tokens recommended)', the load-on-activation reason matches 'The full SKILL.md body is loaded when the skill is activated' and the Body content note, the figures are recommendations rather than measurements, and the slot default (slots.md:25, instructions-skills.md:5-15) sets no authoring budget, so skills-library/extends holds.

practices.statement: The required description field is 1-1024 characters and should say both what the skill does and when to use it, with specific keywords that help the agent match tasks.
practices.quote: Should describe both what the skill does and when to use it
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the description in SKILL.md frontmatter drives model invocation. The listing cap is 1,536 characters, with a startup warning when a description is truncated (CHANGELOG 2.1.295 L5744). Codex: the SKILL.md description in .agents/skills.
practices.change: Cap descriptions of skills shared between Claude Code and Codex at the portable 1024 characters, which is stricter than Claude Code's 1,536-character listing cap. Each description should state what the skill does and when to use it, with task keywords. Add the length check to scripts/validate.py.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears exactly under 'description field', next to 'Must be 1-1024 characters' and 'Should include specific keywords that help agents identify relevant tasks', so the statement is faithful and 'asserted' is right, and a rule on description content extends a default that only governs which skills load and how (skills-library/extends).

practices.statement: A skill name must be 1-64 lowercase alphanumeric characters and hyphens, with no leading, trailing or consecutive hyphens, and must match its parent directory name.
practices.quote: Must match the parent directory name
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the skill directory plus the name frontmatter, with nested-directory clashes namespaced <dir>:<name> (layer page route). Codex: .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md.
practices.change: Make the spec's naming rules (lowercase, hyphens, name equals directory) a requirement for skills we author or pin. Enforce them with skills-ref validate (see the Validation practice) so the same directory works under both .claude/skills and .agents/skills.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears exactly under 'name field', whose bullets give 'Must be 1-64 characters', lowercase alphanumerics (a-z, 0-9) and hyphens, no leading or trailing hyphen and no '--', matching the statement; 'asserted' is right, and a naming requirement extends the library default (skills-library/extends).

practices.statement: Each references/ file should cover one focused topic, because agents load these files on demand and smaller files use less context.
practices.quote: Keep individual reference files focused. Agents load these on demand, so smaller files mean less use of context.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: the agent reads a skill's reference files with the Read tool only when the body points to them. Codex: on-demand file reads from the skill directory (not verified in the client).
practices.change: State in the skills-library default that a skill splits its reference material into one file per topic, read on demand. Our claude-native-practice skill already does this (layer pages of 14-107 lines, observed now); apply the same rule to new skills.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears exactly under 'references/', the paraphrase (focused files, loaded on demand, less context) is faithful, nothing is measured, and file-splitting guidance extends the library default; the change's 'already does this' claim also holds (wc -l, observed now: reference pages 14-107 lines, SKILL.md 24).

practices.statement: Other files should be referenced by relative path from the skill root and kept one level deep from SKILL.md, avoiding chains of references that lead to further references.
practices.quote: Keep file references one level deep from SKILL.md. Avoid deeply nested reference chains.
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: relative Markdown links in SKILL.md, followed with Read. Codex: the same file layout under .agents/skills.
practices.change: Add the one-level reference rule to our skill authoring practice. Observed now: claude-native-practice/SKILL.md lines 8-14 send the agent to reference/slots.md, which then links each layer page, a two-hop chain. Either link every layer page directly from SKILL.md or record the two-hop index as an accepted exception.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears under 'File references', verbatim apart from whitespace (inline code splits 'SKILL.md .'), the relative-path part matches the section's first line ('use relative paths from the skill root'), 'asserted' is right and skills-library/extends holds; the change's two-hop observation is accurate (SKILL.md:8-14 points to reference/slots.md, whose rows link the layer pages).

practices.statement: Scripts bundled in scripts/ should be self-contained or document their dependencies, print helpful error messages and handle edge cases gracefully.
practices.quote: Be self-contained or clearly document dependencies
practices.native_mechanism: Claude Code: skill scripts run through the Bash tool, optionally pre-approved by the skill's allowed-tools. Codex: shell execution of the skill's scripts.
practices.change: Extend the skills-library adoption check: every script in an authored or manifest skill declares its dependencies, and on bad input it exits non-zero with an actionable message. Check this in the paired with/without runs the slot already owes.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears exactly under 'scripts/' with the sibling bullets 'Include helpful error messages' and 'Handle edge cases gracefully', so the statement is faithful, 'asserted' is right and skills-library/extends holds, though the change's 'exits non-zero' requirement goes beyond the page's wording.

practices.statement: Skills should be validated with the skills-ref reference library, which checks that SKILL.md frontmatter is valid and follows the naming conventions.

missed_by_reader: Config shape: 'command and mcp_tool handlers are supported. prompt and agent handlers are parsed but skipped.' Our loops-completion route (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/workers.md:66) uses a 'prompt type with an explicit model for judged conditions', so a judged Stop gate never runs on Codex. The reading marks practices 0-3 as clients 'both' without flagging this. On Codex, completion gates must be command or mcp_tool handlers.

Matcher patterns > Tool coverage: 'Treat tool hooks as a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary.' The page shows several fail-open paths. Hosted tools such as WebSearch run neither PreToolUse nor PostToolUse. write_stdin does not re-run PreToolUse. For MCP tool hooks, 'Errors, missing servers, and unavailable tools don't block the operation'. Under Common output fields, a PreToolUse hook that returns unsupported fields 'marks that hook run as failed, reports the error, and continues the tool call'. These matter for the hooks slot, whose default fails closed (onFailure: block). The reading kept only the MCP sentence, as a lead, and skipped the guardrail note.

Review and trust hooks: 'Codex records trust against the hook's current hash, so new or changed hooks are marked for review and skipped until trusted.' Plugin-bundled hooks are not trusted on install, and project-local hooks load only when the project .codex/ layer is trusted. So a new or edited Codex gate silently does not run until it is trusted in /hooks. The reading declared trust review out of scope; this entry disputes that scoping, because an untrusted gate is a loops-completion and hooks quality failure.

practices.statement: A Stop hook that returns decision block with a reason does not reject the turn: it makes the agent continue, with the reason sent as a new user-style continuation prompt. That makes it a completion gate.
practices.quote: decision: "block" doesn’t reject the turn. Instead, it tells Codex to continue and automatically creates a new continuation prompt that acts as a new user prompt
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: Stop hook in hooks.json or config.toml [hooks] returning {"decision":"block","reason":...} (or exit 2 with the reason on stderr). Claude Code: settings Stop hook returning decision block with reason (the slot's named default; Stop and stop_hook_active strings observed in the 2.1.295 binary).
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in Hooks > Stop, whose sentence ends 'using your reason as that prompt text', so the paraphrase is faithful, asserted is right (the page reports no measurement), and agrees holds against the loops-completion default 'Native Stop hook as the completion gate' (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/slots.md:35).

practices.statement: Stop hook input carries stop_hook_active, which tells the gate whether this turn was already continued by a Stop hook, so the gate can bound its own loop.
practices.quote: Whether this turn was already continued by Stop
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: stop_hook_active (plus last_assistant_message) in the Stop and SubagentStop input. Claude Code: stop_hook_active in the Stop hook input (string observed in the 2.1.295 binary); our route already bounds the loop with it plus a continuation cap.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is the verbatim stop_hook_active row of the Hooks > Stop input table, the paraphrase is faithful, asserted is right, and agrees holds against the loops-completion route 'stop_hook_active and the continuation cap bound the loop' (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/workers.md:66).

practices.statement: When several Stop hooks match, any one returning continue false outranks the others' continuation decisions, so a hard-stop gate can end a loop that other gates would extend.
practices.quote: If any matching Stop hook returns continue: false, that takes precedence over continuation decisions from other matching Stop hooks.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: the Stop hook common output field continue:false. Claude Code: the continue:false common hook output field on Stop (its precedence over decision:block was not verified against Claude docs or the binary in this run).
practices.change: Put the continuation cap in its own Stop hook that returns continue: false once the cap is reached, separate from the check gates that return decision: block. Before relying on it, confirm on Claude Code 2.1.295 that continue: false outranks another hook's block.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in Hooks > Stop and paraphrased faithfully, asserted is right, and extends holds because the loops-completion route (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/workers.md:66) names a continuation cap but no separate continue:false hook or its precedence, while the Claude Code precedence stays unverified, as the reading itself states.

practices.statement: Subagents get their own completion gate: a SubagentStop hook, matched on agent_type, can return decision block to send the subagent for another focused pass.
practices.quote: To ask Codex to continue the subagent flow, return:
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: SubagentStop hook with the matcher on agent_type and input agent_id, agent_transcript_path, stop_hook_active and last_assistant_message. Claude Code: SubagentStop hook, or a Stop hook in the agent's frontmatter, which runs as SubagentStop (SubagentStop and agent_transcript_path observed in the 2.1.295 binary).
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in Hooks > SubagentStop, where the same section states 'matcher is applied to agent_type' and gives the example reason 'Run one more focused pass inside the subagent.', asserted is right, and agrees holds because <pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/workers.md:70 already routes Workflow children through a frontmatter Stop hook that runs as SubagentStop.

practices.statement: After compaction, a SessionStart hook matching source compact re-injects must-keep context before the next model request, including when auto-compaction happens mid-turn.
practices.quote: After Codex compacts a root session, SessionStart hooks that match source: "compact" run before the next model request.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: SessionStart hook with matcher compact returning hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext. Claude Code: SessionStart hook with matcher compact (the route named in our context-compaction default).
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in Hooks > SessionStart, which adds that this 'also applies when automatic compaction happens in the middle of a turn', asserted is right, and agrees holds against the context-compaction route 're-inject must-keep state with a SessionStart hook matching compact' (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/token-efficiency.md:9).

practices.statement: Keep hook-injected context short, because context from several hooks and plugins adds up and degrades the model. Codex caps each hook-output message at roughly 2,500 tokens by default, saves the rest to a file and shows a head-and-tail preview.
practices.quote: Keep hook and plugin context concise. Context from multiple hooks and plugins adds up and can degrade model performance.
practices.section: Large hook output (under Common output fields)
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: the per-handler additionalContextLimit (default 2,500 tokens; 0 means no cap) with spilling to <temp_dir>/hook_outputs. Claude Code: no per-handler additionalContextLimit (string absent from the 2.1.295 binary), so each hook script must bound its own output; Claude's built-in cap was not verified in this run.
practices.change: Add a hook-context budget to the route: every hook that injects context (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, SubagentStart) prints bounded additionalContext, sized against the Codex 2,500-token default, and points to a file for larger material. On Codex, keep additionalContextLimit at its default and never set it to 0 unless the hook enforces a hard cap.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in Common output fields > Large hook output and output-compression/extends hold, but the statement misstates documented behavior: the page says Codex 'saves the full text under <temp_dir>/hook_outputs/<session_id>/<uuid>.txt' (the full text, not 'the rest') and that context 'can degrade model performance', which the statement hardens to 'degrades the model'.

practices.statement: Background (async) hooks cannot block, approve, rewrite or continue anything, and their output arrives only at the next safe point, so policy checks and turn-continuation gates must stay synchronous.
practices.quote: Background hooks can’t block, approve, rewrite, or otherwise control the operation that triggered them. Use synchronous hooks for tool policies, permission decisions, prompt rejection, or turn continuation.
practices.section: Run hooks in the background > How background hooks run
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: "async": true on a command handler (up to eight background hooks run at once per session; unfinished ones are cancelled at session end). Claude Code: "async": true on a command hook (2.1.295 schema text: "If true, hook runs in background without blocking"), plus asyncRewake.
practices.change: State in the hooks route that guard hooks and Stop or SubagentStop completion gates always run synchronously, with no async or asyncRewake. Use async: true only for logging, telemetry and context hooks whose output may arrive later.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in Run hooks in the background > How background hooks run, which also says output arrives 'at the next safe point'; Limitations confirms up to eight concurrent background hooks per session and cancellation at session end; asserted is right; and extends holds because the hooks default (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/native-clients.md:64-66) states no synchronous requirement.

practices.statement: A PostToolUse hook can check a tool result after the fact: decision block replaces the result with the hook's feedback, and additionalContext adds developer context, so the model fixes the problem on its next step.
practices.quote: For this event, decision: "block" doesn’t undo the completed Bash command. Instead, Codex records the feedback, replaces the tool result with that feedback, and continues the model
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: PostToolUse hook matched on Bash, apply_patch/Edit/Write or an MCP tool name, either as a command or as an mcp_tool hook (the page's example sends each patch to a scanner MCP tool). Claude Code: PostToolUse hook returning decision block with reason or hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext; mcp_tool hooks are present in the 2.1.295 binary.
practices.change: Add a verification route to the hooks slot: a synchronous PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write (Codex: apply_patch, Edit or Write) runs a fast deterministic check, such as lint or typecheck on the touched file, and returns decision: block with the failure as its reason. The full-suite gate stays with the Stop hook. This is unmeasured: it needs a paired run before it becomes a default.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is a verbatim prefix of the Hooks > PostToolUse sentence ending 'continues the model from the hook-provided message', the same section says additionalContext 'is added as extra developer context', MCP tool hooks > Configure an MCP tool hook confirms the scanner example (matcher 'Write|Edit', type mcp_tool), asserted is right, and extends holds because the hooks default (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/native-clients.md:64) has no post-edit verification route.

sources.title: Custom instructions with AGENTS.md | ChatGPT Learn
missed_by_reader: Customize fallback filenames: when a repository already uses another instruction filename (e.g. TEAM_GUIDE.md, .agents.md), list it in project_doc_fallback_filenames in ~/.codex/config.toml; names not on the list are ignored for discovery, and Codex must be restarted to load the change (sections 'Customize fallback filenames' and Troubleshoot 'Codex ignores fallback names').

Use CODEX_HOME for a separate profile, such as a project-specific automation user (`CODEX_HOME=$(pwd)/.codex codex exec ...`), and when guidance is missing run `echo $CODEX_HOME` to confirm Codex reads the home you edited (sections 'Customize fallback filenames' and Troubleshoot 'Profile confusion').

Confirm the detected project root with `codex status` when nothing loads (it is typically the Git root; with none, Codex checks only the current directory), and when wrong guidance appears, look for an AGENTS.override.md higher in the tree or under Codex home and rename or remove it (section 'How Codex discovers guidance', Project scope; Troubleshoot 'Nothing loads' and 'Wrong guidance appears').

practices.statement: Instruction files form a layered chain: global first, then one file per directory from the project root down to the working directory, joined in that order so that guidance nearer the work comes later and overrides earlier text.
practices.quote: Files closer to your current directory override earlier guidance because they appear later in the combined prompt.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: the AGENTS.md discovery chain (~/.codex, then project root to cwd). Claude Code: the CLAUDE.md hierarchy (user ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, ancestor files concatenated at launch, subdirectory files loaded on demand), with each CLAUDE.md importing @AGENTS.md. Observed now: blueprints/us-equities/CLAUDE.md is exactly `@AGENTS.md`.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'How Codex discovers guidance' (Merge order bullet), and the paraphrase matches the Global-scope and Project-scope bullets, the root-down concatenation and the 'global file first' expected output, except that the page says 'at most one file per directory'; 'asserted' is right, and instruction-files/agrees holds because our nested AGENTS.md layering, imported through CLAUDE.md, fits this chain.

practices.statement: Codex stops adding project instruction files once their combined size reaches project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB by default). When the cap is hit, split guidance across nested directories or raise the limit, so that critical text is not truncated.
practices.quote: Codex skips empty files and stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit defined by project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB by default).
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: the project_doc_max_bytes key in ~/.codex/config.toml (unset on this host, observed now, so 32 KiB applies). Claude Code: no byte cap is named in our records; the memory docs give a writing target of under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md (docs/harness-rules-convergence-20260922.md:110), which is guidance rather than truncation.
practices.change: Record Codex's 32 KiB project_doc_max_bytes as the budget for the AGENTS.md chain in the instruction-files notes, and add a scripts/validate.py check that the longest root-to-subtree chain stays below 32,768 bytes, splitting into nested files rather than raising the cap. Observed now: root 2,331 B plus blueprints/us-equities/AGENTS.md 5,499 B is 7,830 B; ~/.codex/AGENTS.md is 2,809 B. Whether the global file counts toward the cap is unknown.
practices.refute_reason:
The quote is verbatim in 'How Codex discovers guidance', and the split-or-raise advice comes from the same paragraph and from Troubleshoot's 'Instructions truncated ... keep critical guidance intact'; 'asserted' is right, and 'extends' holds because the instruction-files row and its layer page name no byte budget; however, the cap sentence is a standalone paragraph after the discovery list (observed now:

) and says 'files', so both the statement's 'project instruction files' and the reading's note that the cap appears only in the project-scope discussion narrow the page.

practices.statement: Put cross-repository working agreements in the global instruction file in the agent's home directory so that every repository inherits them, and keep repository norms in the project files.
practices.quote: Create persistent defaults in your Codex home directory so every repository inherits your working agreements.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: ~/.codex/AGENTS.md (present on this host, 2,809 bytes, observed now). Claude Code: user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Create global guidance', and the repository-norms half matches 'Repository-level files keep Codex aware of project norms while still inheriting your global defaults' in 'Layer project instructions'; 'asserted' is right, and 'agrees' holds, though the instruction-files layer page notes that the core loads twice (user CLAUDE.md plus the AGENTS.md import), so we also copy cross-repo text into the project file rather than relying only on inheritance.

practices.statement: Codex loads nested guidance only for directories between the project root and the working directory, so specialized rules belong as close to that work as possible, and the agent has to start inside the subtree to pick them up.
practices.quote: Codex stops searching once it reaches your current directory, so place overrides as close to specialized work as possible.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: a nested AGENTS.md or AGENTS.override.md, loaded when Codex starts with `codex --cd <subtree>`. Claude Code: a nested CLAUDE.md (here `@AGENTS.md`) loaded on demand when files there are read, plus paths:-scoped .claude/rules (observed now: .claude/rules/trading.md).
practices.change: Launch Codex lanes whose work sits in a subtree that has its own AGENTS.md (for example blueprints/us-equities) with `--cd <subtree>` or a worktree cwd at that subtree, so the nested file loads natively. Keep the root AGENTS.md prose subtree rule only as the fallback for Codex runs started at the root, which do not load nested files.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim under the h2 'Layer project instructions' (the '## Payments service rules' line above it sits inside the example code block), and the start-in-subtree clause is backed by the `codex --cd services/payments` example and the project-root-to-cwd walk; 'asserted' is right, and 'extends' holds because the instruction-files default says nothing about the Codex launch directory.

practices.statement: An AGENTS.override.md replaces the regular AGENTS.md at the same level, globally or per directory, so a temporary or team-specific override can be applied and later removed without deleting the base file.
practices.quote: Use ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md when you need a temporary global override without deleting the base file.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: AGENTS.override.md, checked before AGENTS.md in each directory. Claude Code: no replace-semantics equivalent was verified. The nearest native features are claudeMdExcludes (skip a file, named in our layer notes) and an additive local CLAUDE.md (not verified on 2.1.295).
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Create global guidance', and the replace semantics, per-directory scope and 'team-specific' wording are backed by the discovery bullets (override checked first, one file per level), the sample tree ('Ignored because an override exists') and 'when specific teams need different rules'; 'asserted' is right, and 'not-covered' holds because neither the index row nor its layer page names an override mechanism.

practices.statement: Review rules for Codex's GitHub code review belong in a Code Review Rules section of the AGENTS.md nearest the code they govern. Each rule should be short, name the behavior to flag and the safe path or exception, and leave formatting and lint to CI.
practices.quote: Keep rules concise, explain the behavior to flag and any safe path or exception, and reserve formatting and lint checks for CI.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: GitHub code review reading a `## Code Review Rules` section in AGENTS.md. Claude Code: reviewers (claude-code-action, /code-review, pr-review-toolkit agents) see project instructions through CLAUDE.md and its @AGENTS.md import. Whether the toolkit agents read that section was not verified.
practices.change: Add `## Code Review Rules` sections to the nested AGENTS.md closest to the governed code (first candidate: blueprints/us-equities/AGENTS.md for trading-gate defects), each naming the behavior to flag and the safe path, with lint left to CI. Leave the root unchanged so the four-rule core stays the only always-loaded root text (G6a). Count the effect in the owed paired same-delta review run.
practices.refute_reason:
The quote is verbatim (a hard-wrapped prose

after the example code block in 'Add code review rules') and the paraphrase is faithful, but the page scopes the section to 'For Codex code review in GitHub', while the pr-review-pre-cue default is the Claude pr-review-toolkit agents and the reading itself leaves unverified whether they read the section, so 'extends' does not hold against that default.

practices.statement: After changing instruction files, check which files the agent actually loaded and in what order: ask it to list its instruction sources, or audit the session log, rather than assuming discovery worked.
practices.quote: To audit which instruction files Codex loaded, opt into a plaintext TUI log with codex -c log_dir=./.codex-log and check ./.codex-log/codex-tui.log
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: the `codex -c log_dir=...` TUI log, session-*.jsonl, or a prompt asking it to summarize the active instructions. Claude Code: `/memory` and `/context` (docs/harness-defaults.md:68) and the InstructionsLoaded hook event.
practices.change: Add a load read-back to the instruction-files default: after any instruction-file edit, in a new session, confirm the loaded files with `/memory` or `/context` for Claude and with the Codex TUI log or `codex debug prompt-input` (the latter from docs/harness-defaults.md:68, not this page). Prefer these rendered-input checks to the page's model self-summary.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is a verbatim prefix of a 'Verify your setup' bullet that continues ', or inspect the most recent session-*.jsonl file', and with the precedence-order summary and the `--cd subdir` check the paraphrase is faithful; 'asserted' is right, and 'extends' holds against the instruction-files row, which has no read-back step, although docs/harness-defaults.md:68 already lists `/memory`, `/context` and `codex debug prompt-input` as capability-check steps.

practices.statement: Codex rebuilds the instruction chain at the start of every run or TUI session and keeps no cache, so instruction edits take effect only in a new run, and a restart is the fix for stale guidance.
practices.quote: Codex rebuilds the instruction chain on every run (and at the start of each TUI session), so there is no cache to clear manually.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: a new `codex` or `codex exec` run, or a new TUI session. Claude Code: CLAUDE.md files are read at session start; our check runs in a session started after the edit (docs/decisions/2026-09-26-harness-rules-cleanup.md:199). Mid-session reload on 2.1.295 was not verified.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Verify your setup' after 'If instructions look stale, restart Codex in the target directory', and the paraphrase is faithful except that the discovery intro hedges the TUI case ('usually means once per launched session'), so 'only in a new run' slightly overstates it; 'asserted' is right, and 'not-covered' holds because the index row and its layer page say nothing about reload timing.

practices.section: Example: Autofix CI failures in GitHub Actions
