sources.title: Plugins
missed_by_reader: Plugin hook scripts must already exist in the execution environment ('installing a plugin on the web doesn't deploy those scripts'), and plugin hooks must be reviewed and trusted before they run (Hooks item under 'Use plugins from a supported surface'). This bears on the hooks slot, and the reading skipped only the trust sentence.

Plugin capabilities that run through a Codex host stay under that host's sandbox and approval policy ('When a plugin capability runs through a Codex host, the host's sandbox and approval policy applies', under 'How permissions and data sharing work'). The reading scoped this section out, but it bears on the sandbox and settings-permissions slots.

Uninstalling removes only the plugin bundle, so separately connected MCP server integrations must be disconnected on their own ('Separately connected MCP server integrations remain connected in ChatGPT until you disconnect them there', under 'Remove a plugin'). The reading also scoped this section out.

practices.statement: A plugin is the unit that packages reusable workflow capability, bundling skills and MCP servers (and optionally hooks and browser extensions) for install from a shared directory.
practices.quote: Plugins bundle capabilities into reusable workflows in ChatGPT and Codex. They can include skills and MCP servers.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: plugins installed with `codex plugin add` from a configured marketplace, or with /plugins in the CLI (observed in the 0.161.0 help). Claude Code: native plugins that bundle skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers, installed with `claude plugin install <plugin>@<marketplace>` (observed in the 2.1.295 help).
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under Overview, and each element the statement adds is stated on the page (hooks and browser extensions as plugin parts, one universal plugin directory), though the page makes all four parts optional ('can contain one or more of these parts'); asserted is right, and agrees holds in the compatible sense with the plugin-marketplaces default (official catalog first).

practices.statement: After installing a plugin from a marketplace, start a fresh session before relying on its bundled skills or tools, because they only load into new sessions.
practices.quote: Install a plugin from a configured marketplace, then start a new session before using its bundled skills or tools.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: a fresh CLI session after `codex plugin add`. Claude Code: restart after install or update (`claude plugin update` help says "restart required to apply", observed now), or `/reload-plugins` (documented in repo records adoption/skills/lifecycle.md:167 and adoption/bootstrap.md:714, not checked on 2.1.295 in this session).
practices.change: Add an activation step to the plugin-marketplaces route: after `claude plugin install` or `update`, restart or run /reload-plugins, then confirm the bundled skills are listed before relying on them. Codex lanes must launch a fresh session after `codex plugin add` or `codex plugin marketplace upgrade`. Do not reuse a running lane.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim in the Overview's Codex CLI paragraph, and the 'only load into new sessions' clause is backed by the page's 'Bundled skills become available when you start a new chat or CLI session after installation'; asserted is right, and extends holds because the plugin-marketplaces default and route cover pinned sources but no step after install.

practices.statement: Plugins are shared with a project or team by publishing them through a marketplace source such as a repository marketplace.
practices.quote: You can share plugins by publishing them through a marketplace source, such as a repo marketplace for a project or team.
practices.section: Use plugins from a supported surface
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: `codex plugin marketplace` (add, list, upgrade, remove configured marketplaces). Claude Code: `claude plugin marketplace` with marketplace.json, where plugin entries can be pinned by sha. Our layer page rejects packaging our own skills and agents as plugins (R56).
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim and the paraphrase is fair, but agrees fails: publishing your own plugins through a repo marketplace for a project or team is the route this slot rejects ('Packaging our own agents and skills as plugins', R56 reaffirmed, <pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/instructions-skills.md:23 and :26), and the page gives no support even to the Default cell alone (consuming sha-pinned plugin sources), which would make the relation not-covered rather than agrees.

practices.statement: Skills are reusable task instructions that the agent loads on demand, together with their references and helper scripts.
practices.quote: ChatGPT and Codex can load them when needed so they follow the right steps and use the right references or helper scripts for a task.
practices.section: Use plugins from a supported surface
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: skills in .agents/skills or bundled in a plugin. Claude Code: native Agent Skills (SKILL.md with bundled reference files and scripts, loaded on demand), at personal scope or bundled in a plugin.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under 'Use plugins from a supported surface', and the paraphrase matches 'reusable instructions for specific kinds of work ... load them when needed', with 'together with' slightly stretching the page's 'use the right references or helper scripts'; asserted is right, and agrees holds against the native Agent Skills default.

practices.statement: A plugin can ship hooks, which are commands that run at configured lifecycle points in the agent runtime.
practices.quote: Hooks: commands that run at configured lifecycle points in the Codex runtime.
practices.section: Use plugins from a supported surface
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: plugin hooks in the Codex runtime. Claude Code: plugin-bundled hooks alongside settings command hooks; for example, the context-mode plugin supplies lifecycle hooks (repo record docs/token-efficiency-stack.json:914). Our guard hooks remain settings hooks with onFailure block.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim, but the statement widens 'the Codex runtime' to 'the agent runtime' although the page's next sentence says plugin hooks are not supported in cloud-orchestrated ChatGPT Work, and, judged against the whole slot as slots.md:7 directs (layer-page alternatives and rejections), not-covered misdescribes the hooks slot, which ranks the hook-shipping hookify plugin as alternative 1 and rejects plugin mods as guards (<pr-checkout>/.claude/skills/claude-native-practice/reference/native-clients.md:67-68), so this descriptive claim agrees with a settings-hook default the page does not contest.

practices.statement: The source describes MCP servers as the tool layer that defines tools, returns structured data and acts on external systems, with custom UI optional.
practices.quote: They define tools, enforce authentication, return structured data, and perform actions against external systems. They can optionally include custom UI.
practices.section: Use plugins from a supported surface
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: MCP servers bundled in plugins or set in config.toml. Claude Code: MCP servers bundled in plugins or configured with native MCP configuration (tool search defers tools by default).
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim in the MCP servers item, and the paraphrase is faithful apart from dropping 'enforce authentication'; asserted is right, and not-covered holds because the mcp-config-tool-search default and route govern registration, tool deferral and output caps, not what servers do or their optional UI.

practices.statement: Invoke a plugin or one of its bundled skills explicitly by name when you need that specific one, rather than leaving the choice to the model.
practices.quote: Type @ to invoke the plugin or one of its bundled skills explicitly. Use this when you want to be specific about which plugin or skill ChatGPT should use.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex/ChatGPT: an @ mention of the plugin or skill. Claude Code: an explicit slash invocation of the skill, namespaced as /<plugin>:<skill> for plugin skills (for example /context-mode:ctx-doctor in repo records). Otherwise the model invokes skills from their descriptions.
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under 'Choose a specific plugin', and the paraphrase keeps its contrast with 'Describe the task directly' (let ChatGPT choose the installed tools); asserted is right, and agrees holds in the same compatible sense as indexes 0 and 3, because the commands default makes skills the slash-command surface you invoke explicitly, though it covers how commands are defined rather than when to invoke them.

practices.statement: The Codex CLI plugin browser groups plugins by marketplace and lets you turn an installed plugin on or off without uninstalling it.
practices.quote: open a plugin to inspect details, install or uninstall marketplace entries, and press Space on an installed plugin to turn it on or off.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: /plugins browser with a Space toggle. Claude Code: `claude plugin enable` and `disable`, plus `claude plugin details` showing component inventory and projected token cost (all observed in the 2.1.295 help).
practices.refute_reason: The quote appears verbatim under 'Plugin browser in Codex CLI', and 'without uninstalling it' follows from the page listing uninstall and the Space on/off toggle as separate actions; asserted is right, and not-covered holds because nothing in the plugin-marketplaces default, route, alternatives or rejections addresses enabling or disabling installed plugins.

sources.title: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
missed_by_reader: Mechanical checks on the knowledge base: 'Dedicated linters and CI jobs validate that the knowledge base is up to date, cross-linked, and structured correctly.' (We made repository knowledge the system of record)

Recorded evidence and bounded escalation in end-to-end runs: the agent can 'Record a video demonstrating the failure', 'Validate the fix by driving the application', 'Record a second video demonstrating the resolution' and 'Escalate to a human only when judgment is required' (Increasing levels of autonomy)
Humans own acceptance: 'We prioritize work, translate user feedback into acceptance criteria, and validate outcomes.' (What "agent-generated" actually means)

practices.statement: A PR is driven to completion by having the agent review its own change, request specific agent reviews locally and in the cloud, answer all feedback, and loop until every agent reviewer is satisfied.
practices.quote: respond to any human or agent given feedback, and iterate in a loop until all agent reviewers are satisfied
practices.section: Redefining the role of the engineer
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: prompted self-review plus `codex review` (present in codex-cli 0.161.0) and cloud agent review, as the article describes. Claude Code: a native Stop hook (prompt type, or command type running the reviewers) or `/goal`, with the condition that the requested reviewer subagents (pr-review-toolkit, `/code-review`) report no open findings.
practices.change: Add a review-convergence condition to the Stop hook or `/goal` gate for PR-driving runs: the run may stop only when every requested agent reviewer (the pr-review-toolkit pre-cue agents or `/code-review`) reports no open finding at or above the confidence threshold, or the continuation cap is hit. The loop stays inside the native Stop/goal mechanism, not a Ralph-style bash loop.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Redefining the role of the engineer' and the paraphrase and 'asserted' hold, but the page's next words '(effectively this is a Ralph Wiggum Loop)', linked to ghuntley.com/loop/, name the mechanism that workers.md#loops-completion lists under Rejected ('Ralph-style bash loops; ralph-loop plugin as the default'), so the practice as the page states it conflicts with the Stop-hook default; the statement dropped that load-bearing label, and the Stop-hook adaptation belongs in the change field only.

practices.statement: Keep AGENTS.md short (about 100 lines), as a map of pointers into a structured, versioned docs/ directory that is the system of record, so the agent learns where to look next instead of loading one large manual.
practices.quote: A short AGENTS.md (roughly 100 lines) is injected into context and serves primarily as a map, with pointers to deeper sources of truth elsewhere.
practices.section: We made repository knowledge the system of record
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: AGENTS.md. Claude Code: CLAUDE.md importing @AGENTS.md, with deeper material in skills (progressive disclosure), `paths:`-scoped .claude/rules and repository docs.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'We made repository knowledge the system of record'; the statement tracks the adjacent 'structured docs/ directory treated as the system of record' and 'progressive disclosure' sentences; 'asserted' is right because the one-big-AGENTS.md failure is reported without a measurement; and 'agrees' holds against instruction-files, whose route keeps a short core as the only always-loaded text and puts practice in skills, hooks and docs.

practices.statement: Small changes use short-lived lightweight plans; complex work gets execution plans with progress and decision logs, checked into the repository next to completed plans and a technical-debt record.
practices.quote: Active plans, completed plans, and known technical debt are all versioned and co-located, allowing agents to operate without relying on external context.
practices.section: We made repository knowledge the system of record
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: execution-plan files checked into the repository (the article's convention). Claude Code: native plan mode with `plansDirectory` set to a path inside the repository, plus the repository-resident status file and progress notes.
practices.change: Split plans by size. Small changes keep plan mode's short-lived plan. Multi-session work keeps its approved plan in the in-repository `plansDirectory` with a progress log and a decision log section, moves the plan to a completed folder when done, and records open technical debt in a versioned file beside the plans. Agents read all of these at session start.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in the same section and the statement matches 'Ephemeral lightweight plans are used for small changes, while complex work is captured in execution plans with progress and decision logs that are checked into the repository'; 'asserted' is right; and 'extends' holds because the planning-persistence default (JSON status file, progress notes, git commits, plan mode) has no plan-size split, decision log, completed-plans folder or tech-debt tracker.

practices.statement: Architecture and taste invariants are enforced by custom linters and structural tests whose error messages are written as remediation instructions for the agent.
practices.quote: Because the lints are custom, we write the error messages to inject remediation instructions into agent context.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: custom linters and structural tests run by the agent and in CI. Claude Code: a PostToolUse command hook that runs the linter after Edit or Write and returns its message to Claude (exit 2 stderr), plus CI.
practices.change: Beyond guard hooks with `onFailure: "block"`, add PostToolUse lint or check hooks on edited paths. Write every hook and validator failure message as a remediation instruction (what is wrong, the rule, the exact fix or the file to change), because that text goes straight into the agent's context.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Enforcing architecture and taste', 'asserted' is right, and hooks/extends holds against the guard-hook-only default; one caveat: the page ties remediation-instruction error messages to the custom lints ('Because the lints are custom'), not also to structural tests as the statement's 'whose' implies.

practices.statement: Make the running application legible to the agent: one bootable app instance per git worktree, browser automation through Chrome DevTools Protocol skills, and a short-lived per-worktree logs, metrics and traces stack the agent queries with LogQL and PromQL, so it can reproduce bugs and validate fixes itself.
practices.quote: we made the app bootable per git worktree, so Codex could launch and drive one instance per change.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: per-worktree runtime plus skills and the Chrome DevTools Protocol wired into the agent runtime (as described). Claude Code: coordinator-created worktrees, MCP servers (a browser automation server; a Grafana/Loki/Prometheus server for LogQL and PromQL) and skills that drive them.
practices.change: For application repositories, make each coordinator-created worktree bootable as its own isolated instance (its own ports, plus a log and metric endpoint that is torn down with the worktree). Give workers a skill or MCP route to drive that instance and query its logs and metrics, so a fix is validated by running the app, not only by tests.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Increasing application legibility' and the statement matches the page's sentences on CDP 'wired ... into the agent runtime' with skills, a 'local observability stack that's ephemeral for any given worktree', and LogQL/PromQL; 'asserted' is right because the 'upwards of six hours' figure is run length, not the practice's effect; worktrees/extends holds because the default only creates the worktree at its exact base.

practices.statement: Fight agent-replicated drift with garbage collection: encode 'golden principles' in the repository and run recurring background agent tasks that scan for deviations, update quality grades and open small, targeted refactoring PRs. A recurring doc-gardening agent likewise fixes docs that no longer match the code.
practices.quote: On a regular cadence, we have a set of background Codex tasks that scan for deviations, update quality grades, and open targeted refactoring pull requests.
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: recurring background Codex tasks (as described). Claude Code: a systemd --user timer running a bounded `claude -p` with explicit settings, or a GitHub Actions schedule running anthropics/claude-code-action for repository jobs.
practices.change: Add a scheduled cleanup job on the existing scheduler route (a GitHub Actions schedule for repository jobs, or a systemd timer with `claude -p`). It checks the repository against its written principles and its docs against code behaviour, and opens small, single-purpose fix-up PRs. Those PRs land through the existing pre-cue review and landing rules; the article's automerge is not adopted.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Entropy and garbage collection', and 'golden principles' and the recurring 'doc-gardening' agent (in the system-of-record section) are both on the page; 'asserted' is right because '20% of the week' is the prior manual cost, not a measured effect; scheduled-tasks/extends holds, and a GitHub Actions schedule is that slot's stated route for repository jobs.

practices.statement: When the agent fails, treat it as a missing capability, not something to retry harder. Feed review comments and bugs back as docs or tooling, and promote a rule from documentation into code when documentation is not enough.
practices.quote: When documentation falls short, we promote the rule into code
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: AGENTS.md and docs, then custom lints and structural tests that Codex itself writes. Claude Code: CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and skills, then deterministic hooks, scripts/validate.py checks or CI tests.
practices.change: Add a promotion rule to the instruction-files route. When an instruction-file, skill or doc rule is missed again in review, encode it as a deterministic check (hook, lint, validate.py or CI test) whose message states the fix, and keep the prose only as a pointer to that check.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim, the last sentence of 'Enforcing architecture and taste'; the statement faithfully joins it with 'the fix was almost never "try harder"', 'what capability is missing' and 'Review comments, refactoring pull requests, and user-facing bugs are captured as documentation updates or encoded directly into tooling'; 'asserted' is right; and instruction-files/extends holds because the default names files and scoping but no rule-promotion trigger.

practices.statement: The agent gathers its own context and acts through the team's standard tools and repository-embedded skills (gh, local scripts), with humans steering by prompt rather than relaying context. The article describes no separate orchestration framework.
practices.quote: Codex uses our standard development tools directly (gh, local scripts, and repository-embedded skills) to gather context without humans copying and pasting into the CLI.
practices.section: Redefining the role of the engineer
practices.native_mechanism: Codex: repository skills plus CLI tools (gh, scripts). Claude Code: native composition (skills, Bash with gh, subagent definitions, Workflows), with no framework layer.
practices.refute_reason: The quote is verbatim in 'Redefining the role of the engineer' but concerns the agent gathering its own context through gh, local scripts and repository-embedded skills, while the page never discusses orchestration frameworks (its only 'framework' uses are the 'application framework' scaffold and 'Codex's framework for design decisions'), so 'agrees' with orchestration-frameworks rests on silence; the nearest slot is skills-library, and the page's team-written repository-embedded skills extend its personal-scope vendor-manifest default.
